name: Retinitis Punctata Albescens

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for Retinitis Punctata Albescens

criteria.description: Presence of multiple white punctate spots scattered throughout the retina
Progressive nyctalopia (night blindness) starting in childhood or early adulthood
Electroretinogram (ERG) showing reduced rod and cone responses
Family history consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance
Characteristic fundus autofluorescence pattern with hypoautofluorescent spots

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of white punctate retinal spots, progressive night blindness, and abnormal ERG findings
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Genetic testing can confirm diagnosis but is not mandatory

pathognomonic.notes: Characteristic scattered white dots on fundus examination
searchTerms: multiple small white spots in retina

pathognomonic.notes: Early symptom reflecting rod photoreceptor dysfunction
ERG shows reduced rod and cone responses
searchTerms: eye test showing rod and cone dysfunction
retinal electrical abnormalities affecting rods and cones

common.notes: Gradual central vision loss in later stages

occasional.notes: Dyschromatopsia may develop with disease progression
Occasional cystoid macular changes detected on OCT
Prolonged recovery of vision in darkness
searchTerms: difficulty seeing in low light initially

rare.notes: Secondary cataract formation in advanced disease
searchTerms: cloudy lens at back of eye
posterior lens opacity causing vision problems

rare.notes: Optic nerve head changes in late stages
Rare complication leading to vitreous hemorrhage

imaging: Fundus photography showing white punctate spots
Optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealing retinal layer abnormalities
genetic: Mutations in RLBP1 gene commonly associated
Other genes implicated include PRPH2 and RDH5
other: Electroretinogram (ERG) with reduced rod and cone responses

distinguishingFeatures: Typical bone-spicule pigmentation rather than white punctate spots
Stationary night blindness rather than progressive
Delayed dark adaptation without progressive vision loss
Distinct ERG pattern with recovery after prolonged dark adaptation
Increased sensitivity to short wavelength light
Characteristic fundus changes different from punctate spots

redFlags: Sudden onset of visual field defects
Presence of vitreous hemorrhage or retinal neovascularization
references: Hamel C. Retinitis pigmentosa. Orphanet J Rare Dis. 2006;1:40.
Fishman GA. Retinitis punctata albescens: clinical features and natural history. Arch Ophthalmol. 1978;96(3):491-496.
